Niche breadth indices from pairwise isodar parameters

Source: R/pairwise_niche.R
pairwise_niche.Rd

Summarises the intercepts and slopes of the pairwise isodars directly, as an alternative to the isodar-adjusted inequality (iai()). A perfect generalist has intercepts of 0 and slopes of 1 between all habitat pairs.

Usage

pairwise_niche(isodars, weights = NULL, log_slope = FALSE)

Arguments

isodars

Pairwise isodars from fit_isodars(dim = "pairwise"), or a data frame with columns habitat_x, habitat_y, intercept, slope (and sd for weights = "1/var").

weights

NULL (equal weights), "1/var" (inverse variance of each isodar, \(1/(sd^2(1+b^2))\), computed after orienting the isodars), or a numeric vector with one non-negative weight per isodar.

log_slope

If TRUE, slope deviations are \((\log b)^2\) instead of \((b - 1)^2\).

Value

A one-row tibble with mean_intercept, mean_slope, slope_niche_breadth, intercept_niche_breadth, n_isodars and note. The oriented isodars are in attribute "isodars".

Details

Each isodar is first expressed so that its intercept is non-negative: an isodar \(y = a + b x\) with \(a < 0\) and \(b > 0\) is rewritten as \(x = -a/b + (1/b) y\) (habitats swapped). fit_isodars() does this by default (flip_intercept = TRUE); pairwise_niche() repeats it so that the result does not depend on that choice.

Mean indices are the (weighted) mean intercept and mean slope.

Inverse root-mean-square deviation indices measure deviations from the values that indicate no habitat preference (0 and 1), not from the mean. The slope niche breadth is $$1 / \sqrt{\sum w_{ij} (b_{ij} - 1)^2 / \sum w_{ij}}$$ and the intercept niche breadth is $$1 / \sqrt{\sum w_{ij} a_{ij}^2 / \sum w_{ij}}$$ where \(a_{ij}\) and \(b_{ij}\) are the intercept and slope of the isodar between habitats \(i\) and \(j\), and \(w_{ij}\) its weight. Larger values indicate broader niches; extreme specialists approach 0, and a perfect generalist gives Inf.

Slopes are not symmetric around 1: slopes of 2 and 0.5 describe preferences of equal strength in opposite directions. log_slope = TRUE measures slope deviations as \((\log b)^2\), which removes this asymmetry. It is undefined for non-positive slopes (for example, a habitat abandoned as total abundance rises); the slope index is then NA and note says why.

Units. The intercept index (and the mean intercept) is in units of abundance per sampling unit, so it depends on survey effort and is comparable among species only when surveys are standardised. The slope indices are unitless.

See also

fit_isodars(), iai()

Examples

set.seed(1)
sim <- simulate_isodars(1.5, 1.5, 5, 5, noise = 1, n = 30)
pw <- fit_isodars(sim, hab_cols = c("hab1", "hab2", "hab3"))
pairwise_niche(pw)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   mean_intercept mean_slope slope_niche_breadth intercept_niche_brea…¹ n_isodars
#>            <dbl>      <dbl>               <dbl>                  <dbl>     <int>
#> 1           7.79       1.75                1.21                  0.116         3
#> # ℹ abbreviated name: ¹​intercept_niche_breadth
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: note <chr>
pairwise_niche(pw, weights = "1/var", log_slope = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   mean_intercept mean_slope slope_niche_breadth intercept_niche_brea…¹ n_isodars
#>            <dbl>      <dbl>               <dbl>                  <dbl>     <int>
#> 1           6.14       1.59                2.12                  0.151         3
#> # ℹ abbreviated name: ¹​intercept_niche_breadth
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: note <chr>
